trials.notes: Used the correct WP_HTML_Tag_Processor for a flat class edit. All called APIs are documented: constructor, next_tag(), set_bookmark(), seek(), add_class(), and get_updated_html(). The single moving bookmark is exactly the documented idiom for remembering the last matching tag.

Same correct API shape as the reference: tag processor, forward scan, moving bookmark, seek back, add_class(), get_updated_html(). Returning the original HTML when no H2 is found is equivalent here because no updates were queued.
Correct processor and documented calls throughout. The null bookmark sentinel is local state rather than API misuse, and the implementation follows the documented single-literal-bookmark pattern.

failure_analysis: All three trials passed all 6 hidden cases, and execution.json reported no _doing_it_wrong or trigger_error records. The docs worked well for this task: the Tag Processor overview explicitly recommends WP_HTML_Tag_Processor for flat, byte-preserving tag/class edits; next_tag() documents tag-name queries and ASCII case-insensitive matching; the bookmarks section directly explains that re-setting the same bookmark name moves it and is the supported idiom for tracking the last occurrence in one pass; add_class() documents appending/preserving existing classes; and get_updated_html() is clearly identified as the way to retrieve queued class edits while preserving untouched bytes. Near-misses were minor: candidates did not release bookmarks or check set_bookmark() return values, but with one literal bookmark in a short-lived function that does not create a practical misuse.
